certainty_reasoning: Patricia Pulham's Y90s biography states the attachment and its span; no letter, diary or statement by Lee or Robinson about the relationship has been read, and Pulham's one citation to Robinson's own writing ('Robinson, 935') concerns the visitors to Casa Paget, not the relationship. Second-hand is a statement about who is talking, not a mark of doubt: Pulham is the standard scholarly account and calls it a romantic friendship without hedging.
summary: Vernon Lee met the poet Mary Robinson in 1880, the year Lee came to public notice with Studies of the Eighteenth Century in Italy, and the two formed what Pulham calls a romantic friendship. Robinson visited Lee's home in Florence and Lee returned the visit in London in 1881, where Robinson introduced her to the Burne-Joneses, Gosse, the Morrises, the Rossettis and Oscar Wilde - which is how Lee entered the London circle this map charts. The attachment ended with Robinson's marriage in 1887 to the orientalist James Darmesteter; Kit Anstruther-Thomson replaced her as Lee's companion that same year.

sources.quote: It is also in 1880 that Lee first met the poet Mary Robinson (1857-1944) with whom she developed a romantic friendship that lasted until Mary married in 1887.
sources.context: Patricia Pulham's Y90s biography of Vernon Lee, in the paragraph on Lee's emergence in 1880. The following sentences record Robinson's account of the visitors to 'Casa Paget' and Lee's return visit to London in 1881, at which she met Wilde.
sources.supports: The relationship, its character as Pulham states it, and both its start and end dates.

sources.quote: In 1881, Lee in turn visited Mary in London. Here she met many of the Robinsons’ friends and acquaintances including the Burne-Joneses, Edmund Gosse (1849-1928), the Morrises, the Rossettis, and Oscar Wilde (1854-1900).
sources.context: Pulham, immediately following. This is the sentence that puts Lee in the Wilde circle and puts Robinson at the door of it: the introductions are Robinson's.

sources.quote: Lee and Robinson met in Florence on 16 October 1880 at a party at Maria Spartali Stillman's and they became steadfast friends and romantic partners for almost eight years – a romantic friendship to which their letters testify (Selected Letters of Vernon Lee, Vols. I and II); and Lee took on the role in Mary's life of a strong companion who at times was both nurturing and domineering. … Lee suffered a long period of depression after the marriage took place in August 1888.
sources.context: The editors' biographical note on Mary Robinson in the standard scholarly edition of Lee's correspondence. It states the relationship's character, its exact beginning and its length without hedging, and cites the letters themselves in Vols. I and II. The elision drops the account of Robinson's proposal to James Darmesteter in 1887 and the two families' objections. Volume III (1890-1896) begins after the attachment ended.
sources.supports: The standard edition stating the relationship as romantic, dating its start exactly, giving its length, and recording Lee's depression after the marriage.
sources.citation_provenance: Editors' note, Vernon Lee's Letters, vol. III (2024), PDF pp. 119-120.
sources.speaker: Sophie Geoffroy and Amanda Gagel, eds.

sources.quote:
The dear sprigs of olive and ilex and spicewood came this morning. They stand in my bedroom in a blue bracken jar and remind me of the January posies you used to bring me from your drives in the Cascine, when you came, all keen outer air & crisp green things, into the salon where I would be reading German Mystics over the fire … A great packet of my poor foolish sad little old letters, so young, so senties, poor little unhappy things, was left at the door one day by a nameless young woman. I have only just now dared to glance at them – for one must not glance at Eurydice in Hades. When you know of some very discreet, honourable & yet good natured person who could take charge of your packet, let me know and she shall have it. … Ever your loving old friend

Molly
sources.context: Mary Robinson - by then Mme Darmesteter - to Vernon Lee, Christmas Eve 1893, five years after the marriage. Two things at once: the tenderness of the memory, and the two women arranging the return of each other's old love letters through discreet intermediaries. 'Senties' is Robinson's French, glossed by the editors as 'emotional'; 'the Mouse' elsewhere on the page is Lee's name for her when they were young. The elisions drop a passage on Lee's book and the Revue de Paris, and Robinson's remark about her letters to Symonds. The original is at the Bibliothèque Nationale de France, Anglais 243.
sources.supports: Robinson's own voice on the relationship and on its aftermath - the surviving affection, and the mutual retrieval of the love letters that documented it.
sources.citation_provenance: Robinson to Lee, Christmas Eve 1893, Vernon Lee's Letters, vol. III (2024), PDF pp. 490-491. The edition's own note to this letter reads "Bibliothèque Nationale de France, Manuscrits, Anglais 243, Correspondance de Mary Robinson IV, Lettres de Mary Robinson à Vernon Lee (Violet Paget) 1887-1933", and adds that "Mary Robinson's letters to Vernon Lee are now held at the Bibliothèque Nationale de France, Manuscrits, Paris".
sources.speaker: Mary Robinson (Mme Darmesteter), letter to Vernon Lee

sources.quote: At the time that Levy became acquainted with her, Lee had been in a romantic relationship with the poet and novelist Agnes Mary Robinson (called Mary) since at least the autumn of 1880. When Vernon Lee was in London she stayed with the Robinsons, and when Mary was in Florence she stayed at the Pagets' villa, sharing a room with Lee.
sources.context: Beckman, incidentally, while setting up Levy's own attachment to Lee.
sources.supports: Independent secondary attestation of the Lee-Robinson relationship and its start date, from a biographer of a third party with no stake in the question.

null_findings.finding: The copy available is Volume III (1890-1896) of Lee's letters; the attachment ran 1880-1888, so Lee's own account of it is in Vols. I and II, not held here. Vol. III carries the editors' biographical note and one letter from Robinson's side in 1893. A whole-volume search finds no letter addressed to Robinson in it: 'Robinson' appears on 70 of 815 pages, almost all editorial apparatus, bibliography and archive listings.
